utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Court Deputy, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-76-I, the Prosecutor versus Mirko Norac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Mark Ierace. I am the senior trial attorney in this matter. I appear together with Mr. Anura Meddegoda, trial attorney; and case manager, Lakshmie Walpita.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Zeljko Olujic, attorney-at-law from the Republic of Croatia, appearing here for the Initial Appearance of Mr. Mirko Norac. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Norac, would you please stand up. I will ask you some questions. Can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: May I have your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mirko Norac. My nickname is Kevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is the date upon which you believe you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 19th of September, 1967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And where did you live before you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I was arrested, my address was Vukovacka Street 27 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. We are here this afternoon for the Initial Appearance of the accused in accordance with the Rule 62 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence upon his coming to the Tribunal. The accused was indicted by the Prosecution on the 11th May 2004, and he's currently serving a sentence of 12 years' imprisonment imposed on him by the Croatian court for crime unrelated to the indictment in the case before this Tribunal. I shall inform the parties that this case has been assigned by order of the President to the Trial Chamber I, of which I am a member and the Pre-Trial Judge of this case. Mr. Olujic, has your client received a copy of the indictment in a language which he understands?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my client, as early as on the 9th of June of this year, received the indictment, when he was on remand of the municipal court in Rijeka. He received the indictment in a language he understands. Which means that the indictment had previously been translated into the Croatian language. Following consultation with me, he understood the indictment in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you mean you have a chance to go over it with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, precisely. We've had an opportunity to go through the indictment, and we have indeed done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Does your client fully understand the nature of the procedure and his rights, as well as the contents of the indictment, or is he aware of the nature of the allegation made against him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Mirko Norac is entirely familiar with the indictment and with the facts therein, as well as all the regulations referred to by my learned friend and colleague who put the indictment together. He has understood the indictment, and he knows what he's being charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. However, since this is the first time for him to appear in this Tribunal, I will have Madam Court Deputy to read out Article 21 of the Statute of the Tribunal and the whole indictment to him. Madam Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Article 21, rights of the accused. All persons shall be equal before the International Tribunal. In the determination of charges against him, the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing, subject to Article 22 of the Statute. The accused shall be presumed innocent until proven guilty according to the provisions of the present Statute. In the determination of any charges against the accused pursuant to the present Statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees in full equality: A: To be informed promptly and in detail in a language which he understands of the nature and cause of the charges against him; B: To have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and to communicate with counsel of his own choosing; C: To be tried without undue delay; D: To be tried in his presence and to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing; to be informed, if he does not have legal assistance, of this right; and to have legal assistance assigned to him, in any case where the interests of justice so require, and without payment by him in any such case if he does not have sufficient means to pay for it; E: To examine, or have examined, the witnesses against him and to obtain the attendance and examination of witnesses on his behalf under the same conditions as witnesses against him; F: To have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in the International Tribunal; G: Not to be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And the indictment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to her authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia charges Mirko Norac with crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war, as set forth below: Mirko Norac was born on 19th September 1967 in Otok, in the municipality of Sinj, in the Republic of Croatia. In August 1990, Mirko Norac joined the Ministry of Interior ("the MUP"). In September of the same year, he became a member of the Lucko Anti-Terrorist Unit. On the 12th or 13th of September, 1991, Mirko Norac was appointed Commander of the 118th Brigade of the Croatian army or the Hrvatska Vojska, also known as HV. In November 1992, Mirko Norac was appointed Commander of the 6th Guards Brigade of the HV. In 1993, the 6th Guards Brigade was renamed the 9th Guards Motorised Brigade. He remained Commander of the 9th Guards Motorised Brigade at the time of the Croatian military operation in the Medak Pocket, known as the Medak Pocket operation. During the Medak Pocket operation, he was appointed Commander of Sectors 1, which was a combat group formed for the purposes of conducting the operation. In 1994, Mirko Norac was promoted to the rank of Brigadier and appointed Commander of the Gospic Operational Zone (Military District). He held that rank and remained in that position until the 25th of September, 1995, when President Franjo Tudjman promoted him to the rank of Major General. On the 15th of March, 1996, Mirko Norac was appointed Commander of the Knin Corps District. On the 29th of September, 2000, Mirko Norac was discharged from the HV. Individual and superior criminal responsibility. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mirko Norac is individually responsible for the crimes charged against him in the indictment pursuant to Articles 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Individual responsibility includes planning, instigating, ordering, or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation, or execution of any acts or omissions set forth in the indictment. Mirko Norac, by virtue of his high-ranking position as a Colonel in the HV and Commander of the 9th Guards Motorised Brigade of the HV and Sector 1, from the 9th to the 17th of September, 1993, played a central role in developing, planning, ordering and/or executing the Medak Pocket operation, during which serious violations of international humanitarian law and crimes against humanity were committed, as alleged in this indictment. Mirko Norac, at all times relevant to this indictment, held the position of Commander of the 9th Guards Motorised Brigade of the HV with the rank of Colonel. The 9th Guards Motorised Brigade of the HV was one of the constituent units of Sector 1 of the Gospic Operational Zone and the main HV unit involved in the Medak Pocket Operation. Mirko Norac, as Commander of Sector 1, was empowered to issue orders, and in fact did issue orders. His responsibilities include planning, deploying, directing, executing and monitoring the activities of all sub-units and subordinate formations comprising Sector 1. This includes the 9th Guards Motorised Brigade, the Gospic Home Guard battalion, the Lovinac Home Guard Battalion, units of the 111th Brigade and units of the Special Forces of the MUP. Mirko Norac is also, or alternatively, criminally responsible as a superior for the acts of his subordinates pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. A superior is criminally responsible for the acts of his subordinates, if the superior knew, or had reason to know, that his subordinates were about to commit such acts, or had done so, and the superior failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts, or to punish the perpetrators thereof. Mirko Norac, by the virtue of his high-ranking position as a Colonel in the HV and the Commander of the 9th Guards Motorised Brigade of the HV and Sector 1, had the power, authority, and responsibility to prevent or punish serious violations of international humanitarian law committed during the Medak Pocket operation. Mirko Norac not only had reason to know that, during the Medak Pocket operation, various subordinates under his operational control were responsible for persecuting and killing of Serb civilians and surrendered soldiers and the plunder and destruction of buildings and property, but he in fact knew of such acts. Mirko Norac failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent such acts, or to punish the perpetrators thereof. General allegations. At all times relevant to this indictment, a state of armed conflict existed in the Krajina region of the Republic of Croatia in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. At all times relevant to this indictment, the accused Mirko Norac was required to abide by the laws and customs governing the conduct of war, including Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions of 1949. The acts or omissions alleged against the accused in this indictment which constitute crimes against humanity are crimes punishable under Article 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal, and were part of a widespread and systematic attack directed against a civilian population, specifically the Serb population of the Medak Pocket. In this indictment, every reference to "Croatian forces" means and includes the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, being the HV, and also units of the MUP that participated in the Medak Pocket operation. All references to the Medak Pocket operation means and includes all operations conducted by Croatian forces in and immediately around the area of the Medak Pocket, as described in paragraph 27 below. The general allegations contained in paragraph 13 to 17 are re-alleged and incorporated into each of the related charges set out below. Count 1 (persecutions): Before and during the Croatian military operation in the Medak Pocket, from the 9th of September to or on or about the 17th of September, 1993, Mirko Norac, acting individually and/or in concert with others, including Janko Bobetko and Rahim Ademi, planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, or execution of persecutions of Serb civilians of the Medak Pocket on racial, political or religious grounds. In so far as the accused is responsible for criminal behaviour constituting the crime of persecutions pursuant to Article 7(1) of the Statute, his responsibility is established, inter alia, by evidence of his presence at the relevant time in the areas where such behaviour occurred, his ensuing awareness of the behaviour, steps taken by him to restrict access to the area to his subordinates, and the resulting inference that his behaviour could not have occurred in such a widespread or systematic manner unless it was a consequence of his orders. The crime of persecutions was perpetrated through the following: The unlawful killing of Serb civilians and captured and/or wounded soldiers from the Medak Pocket. As illustrative examples, details of some of those killed are provided in the First Schedule to this indictment; Cruel and inhumane treatment of Serb civilians and captured and/or wounded soldiers from the Medak Pocket, by inter alia, causing serious injuries by means of shooting, stabbing, cutting of fingers, severe beatings with rifle butts, burning with cigarettes, jumping on bodies, tying bodies to a car and dragging them along the road, mutilation and other forms of mistreatment. As an illustrative example, details of some of these acts of cruel and inhumane treatment referred to herein are set out in the Second Schedule to this indictment; Terrorising the predominantly Serb civilian population of the Medak Pocket by, inter alia, the mutilation and desecration of the body of Boja Pjevac; the public killing of Boja Vujnovic, by burning her alive whilst mocking her; expressing an intention to kill all civilians; placing racist graffiti on buildings; and leaving sinister and menacing messages on a destroyed building, all of which resulted in the civilian population being force today abandon their homes and property and to leave the area permanently; The destruction of personal property belonging to Serb civilians of the Medak Pocket, in that on or after the 9th of September 1993, the Croatian forces in the area systematically destroyed up to 164 homes and approximately 148 other buildings (and the contents thereof) by the use of explosives and fire, and as further described in paragraphs 38 to 40 of this indictment. This destruction continued unabated after the cease-fire of 15th September was put into effect and continued until the final withdrawal of the Croatian forces on the 17th of September, 1993. As an illustrative example, some villages, hamlets, or areas where acts of plunder of property were committed are set out in the Third Schedule to this indictment. The systematic plunder of Serb civilian property during and after the military operation in the Medak Pocket by elements of the Croatian forces, in conjunction with Croatian civilians, who unlawfully removed personal goods, such as electrical goods and furniture from buildings that were or about to be destroyed, removed animals and farm equipment, dismantled buildings, and carried parts thereof away by truck, and as further described. As an illustrative example, some villages, hamlets, or areas where acts of plunder of property were committed are set out in the Third Schedule of the indictment. Alternatively, Mirko Norac knew, or had reason to know, that Croatian forces under his command, direction, and/or control, or subordinated to him, were committing the acts described in paragraph 20 above, or had done so. Mirko Norac failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the commission of such acts or punish the perpetrators thereof. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. By these acts and omissions, Mirko Norac did commit: Count 1: A crime against humanity, namely, persecutions on political, racial, or religious grounds, punishable under Article 5(h), read with Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Count 2 and 3 (murder). Between the 9th of September and about the 17th of September, 1993, Mirko Norac knew, or had reason to know, that Croatian forces under his command, direction and/or control, or subordinated to him, were engaged in the unlawful killing of Serb civilians living in the Medak Pocket and Serb soldiers who were captured and/or wounded, or had done so. Mirko Norac failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the commission of such acts or pressure the perpetrators thereof. Particulars of some of the killed civilians and soldiers hors d'combat are contained in the First Schedule to this indictment. By these acts and omissions, Mirko Norac did commit: Count 2: A crime against humanity, namely murder, punishable under Article 5(a), read with Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Count 3: A violation of the laws or customs of war, namely murder, as recognised by Common Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Convention of 1949, punishable under Article 3, read with Article 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Count 4. (Plunder of property). From the 9th of September to on or about the 17th of September, 1993, property of Serb civilians living in the Medak Pocket was plundered. Mirko Norac, acting individually and/or in concert with others, including Janko Bobetko and Rahim Ademi, planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of the plunder of property of Serb civilians of the Medak Pocket. As an illustrative example, some villages, hamlets, or areas where acts of plunder or property were committed are set out in the Third Schedule to this indictment. Alternatively, Mirko Norac knew, or had reason to know, that the Croatian forces under his command, direction and/or control, or subordinated to him, were committing the acts described in paragraph 23 above, or had done so. Mirko Norac failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the commission of such acts or punish the perpetrators thereof. By these acts and omissions, Mirko Norac did commit: Count 4: A violation of the laws or customs of war, plunder of public or private property, punishable under Article 3(e), read with Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Count 5 (wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages). From the 9th of September to on or about the 17th of September, 1993, most Serb villages of the Medak Pocket were destroyed. Mirko Norac, acting individually and/or in concert with others, including Janko Bobetko and Rahim Ademi, planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation, or execution of the destruction of property of Serb civilians of the Medak Pocket. As an example, some villages, hamlets, or areas where acts of wanton destruction were committed are set out in the Third Schedule to this indictment. Alternatively, Mirko Norac knew, or had reason to know, that Croatian forces under his command, direction and/or control, or subordinated to him, were committing the acts described in paragraph 25 above, or had done so. Mirko Norac failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the commission of such acts or punish the perpetrators thereof. By these acts and omissions, Mirko Norac did commit: Count 5: A violation of the laws or customs of war, namely wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages, punishable under Article 3(b) read with Articles 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Statement of the facts: The Medak Pocket was approximately four to five kilometres wide and five to six kilometres long and consisted of the localities of Divoselo, Citluk, and part of Pocitelj and numerous small hamlets. It was situated within it's self-proclaimed Republika Srpska Krajina (the Republic of Serbian Krajina, hereinafter referred to as "the RSK") to the south of the city of Gospic in the Republic of Croatia. It was primarily a rural area with a combination of forest and open fields. Prior to the attack, approximately 400 Serb civilians inhabited the area. Following multi-party elections in Croatia 1990, on the 25th of June 1991, Croatia declared its independence. For some months prior to that, an armed conflict had erupted between Croatian Serbs and Croatian forces. In September 1991, the Croatian Government stated that the Croatian Serbs and the JNA controlled about one third of the territory of Croatia. On the 19th of December, 1991, the Assembly of the Serbian autonomous region of Krajina, together with Serbs from other parts of Croatia, declared independence from Croatia and formed the RSK, with its own military force, the Srpska Vojska Krajina (the Serbian Army of Krajina, or "SVK"). In February 1992, following the Vance Plan, the United Nations Security Council established under its authority a United Nations Protection Force, also known as "UNPROFOR", that was to be deployed in United Nations Protected Areas ("UNPA's") in Croatia. The UNPAs were areas in Croatia where Serbs constituted the majority, or a substantial minority, of the population and where intercommunal tensions had led to armed conflict in the recent past. There were four UNPA's, or United Nations Protected Areas: Sectors north, south, east, and west. The Serb-held or disputed territories in Croatia that were outside the UNPA's were generally referred to as "pink zones". The Medak Pocket was situated in such a "pink zone", close to sector south. The Croatian forces launched several military operations against the RSK in 1992 and in 1993. These operations were launched into the UNPA's or adjacent "pink zones" at the Miljevacki Plateau in June 1992, the area of the Maslenica bridge in northern Dalmatia in January 1993 and the Medak Pocket in September 1993. The Croatian attack on the Medak Pocket commenced with shelling of the area in the early morning of the 9th of September 1993. At approximately 0600 hours, Croatian forces comprising HV units from Gospic Operational Zone, including the 9th Guards Brigade, 111th Brigade, Gospic Home Guard Battalion, Lovinac Home Guard Battalion, and units of Special Forces of the MUP, entered the Pocket. After approximately two days of fighting, they had taken control of Divoselo, Citluk, and part of Pocitelj, after which the Croatian advance halted. At this time, Corps General Janko Bobetko was the Chief of Main Staff of the HV, whilst Brigadier Rahim Ademi was acting Commander of the Gospic Operational Zone. Colonel Mirko Norac was the Commander of the 9th Guards Brigade. Following the intervention of international representatives, negotiations at a political and military level between the Croatian and RSK authorities were initiated shortly after the attack, with the objective of achieving a cessation of hostilities and a withdrawal of Croatian forces from the areas captured during the operation. As a result of such negotiations, an agreement was signed on the 15th of September, 1993 by General Mile Novakovic, on behalf of the Serbian side and Major General Petar Stipetic, on behalf of the Croatian side. The latter was ordered to sign the agreement by Janko Bobetko. Under the terms of the agreement, a cease-fire was to take effect at 1200 hours on the 15th of September, 1993, and the Croatian forces were to leave the territory entered on 9th of September, 1993, leaving the Medak Pocket under UNPROFOR control. The Croatian withdrawal from the Medak Pocket was completed at 1800 hours on the 17th of September, 1993. During the Croatian military operation in the Medak Pocket, at least 29 local Serb civilians were unlawfully killed and others sustained serious injury. Many of the killed and wounded civilians were women and elderly people. Croatian forces also killed at least five Serb soldiers who had been captured and/or wounded. Details of the killed civilians and soldiers hors d'combat are contained in the First Schedule to this indictment. Approximately 164 homes and 148 barns and outbuildings, being a majority of buildings in the villages within the Medak Pocket, were destroyed, mostly by fire and explosives, after the Croatian forces had taken effective control. A substantial portion of this destruction took place between the cease-fire on the 15th of September, 1993 and the completion of the Croatian withdrawal at 1800 hours on September 17th, 1993. Between the 9th and 17th of September, 1993, property belonging to Serb civilians was plundered by the Croatian forces, or by persons in civilian clothes under the supervision of the Croatian forces, for anything of value. These included personal belongings, household goods, furniture, household items, farm animals, farm machinery, and other equipment. Serb-owned civilian property that was not subjected to plunder as described above was burned or otherwise destroyed. Household goods and furniture were destroyed, farm machinery was damaged or destroyed with bullets, farm animals were killed and wells were polluted. As a result of these widespread and systematic unlawful acts during the Croatian military operation, the Medak Pocket became uninhabitable. The villages of the Pocket were completely destroyed, thereby depriving the Serbian civilian population of their homes and livelihood. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, madam court deputy. Well, Mr. Olujic, since you have discussed the contents of the indictment fully with your client, does your client know that he must plea to the charges in the indictment within 30 days of the Initial Appearance or, if he so wishes, he can also do so today. Is he ready to enter a plea today?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my client is familiar with his rights under the Rules and Statute of this Tribunal, and he's prepared to enter a plea here today as to each and every individual count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Norac, are you ready to enter pleas to the charges against you in this indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I propose to read out to you just the charge, and then I will ask you: How do you plead to that charge, guilty or not guilty? Your answer in each case should be "guilty" or "not guilty," as the case may be. If you fail to enter a plea, the Chamber will enter a plea of not guilty on your behalf. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's begin. The first count against you is the charge of persecution, being a crime against humanity. How do you plead, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I plead not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Very well. The second count is a charge of murder, as a crime against humanity. How do you plead: Guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I plead not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The third count is another charge of murder, being a violation of laws and customs of war. How do you plead: Guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I plead not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The fourth count is the charge of plunder of public or private property, as a violation of the laws and the customs of war. How do you plead: Guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I plead not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Very well. The fifth count is the charge of wanton destruction of cities, towns, or villages, as a violation of laws or customs of war. How do you plead: Guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Court Deputy, please register that the accused pleads not guilty to all the counts in the indictment against him. You may sit down, please, Mr. Norac. Well, at this stage, I wish to address the issue of the motion for joinder with the case before this Tribunal against General Ademi, filed by the Prosecutor on the 27th May 2004. The purpose of this motion is to seek to join the two cases into one trial so that the accused will be tried together with General Ademi. The reason why we bring this issue up at this point is that the accused are entitled, under Rule 126 bis, to file a response to the motion within 14 days. The accused may wish to consult his Defence counsel before he responds to this motion. But since the counsel was not assigned to him until recently, and since the accused has not yet seen the supporting material, the Chamber hereby orders the Prosecution to disclose the supporting material to the accused within three days as of today. And it decides that the 14 days time limit for filing a response will begin to run from the moment the accused and his counsel have received supporting material. The Chamber will then decide on the motion when we have received the response, if any. Mr. Olujic, do you have any preliminary comment to that motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Namely, it was today that I received the OTP motion for joinder of accused, dated the 27th of May, 2004, today, on the premises of the Tribunal. I've only had the most cursory look at this proposal by my learned friends and colleagues for the OTP. At this point in time, what I can say is that we will be filing a motion about this, in compliance with the deadline you have just given us. If I understand you correctly, Your Honour, the deadline will begin running as soon as we have received all the documents that you have ordered the OTP to disclose within three days. Therefore, whether we shall be filing a response. Of course, this is something that I need to consult my client on. We shall be certain, however, to comply with all the deadlines given by this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there any difficulties on the part of the Prosecution to file the supporting materials, as I said just now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: To serve a copy of that material on the Defence, no, Your Honour, there's no difficulty with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So it's possible for you to furnish those supporting materials by next Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no difficulty with providing a -- some of that documentation, but I'll need to consult with my team before I could confidently assure you that the materials themselves could be provided in three days. If there is some short adjournment during this proceeding, I will consult and inform you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. I think I'll give you 10 or 15 minutes to consider this issue after we finish the next issue. That is, I have to address today the question of detention or remand. The Chamber has been informed that Croatian Government is willing to receive and detain the accused in Croatia if the Chamber should so allow it, under Rule 64, paragraph 2. The Chamber would like to invite the parties to present their views on this matter. Could I turn to the Prosecution on that issue. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position of the Prosecution is that it is appropriate for the accused to be detained by the Republic of Croatia. I say that because relevant -- the relevant background is that the accused is presently serving a sentence in the Republic of Croatia of some 12 years, for offences that predate those that are alleged against him in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my client, General Mirko Norac, unfortunately has received his sentence by a Croatian court, and the sentence is 12 years' imprisonment. This is a valid sentence and it has already taken effect. Under circumstances I don't think this Honourable Tribunal has any reason to believe that there would be any misuse or undue favour shown by the Croatian courts or any of the Croatian authorities in relation to my client. In addition to which Your Honour please allow me to also refer to resolutions passed by the United Nations and its body, the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal, the constitutional law on cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal, passed and adopted by the Republic of Croatia, all of which serves to guarantee to this Court control over any potential moves by the Croatian courts, even in case of a valid final sentence. I would like to add something else too. General Mirko Norac surrendered to the Croatian court and to this Court, without any sort of problems, and he has already been sentenced, as I've pointed out before. Therefore, there is no reason for General Mirko Norac to leave this courtroom today -- not to leave this courtroom today and go back to Croatia to serve his sentence, and he will always remain available to you, at all times. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, since the Prosecution needs some time to consider the time limits of the disclosure, and since this issue is a major issue, and I think it should be dealt with by the whole Chamber. So we'll take a break for 15 minutes. We'll adjourn at 10 minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, are you ready to give me a definite answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In one sense of the meaning of the word, yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much for that opportunity. I have consulted with the relevant people. I cannot be confident that we could have a set of the supporting material, with necessary redactions, available by Tuesday. If a copy in B/C/S is required as well for those documents not in Croatian. So, Your Honour, I can, I think, say with confidence that a set in the original language of the documents, with redactions, could be provided to the Defence, to my learned colleague, by Tuesday afternoon, and certainly some of the documents which were not in B/C/S could be provided by that date as well. It may be, however, that we will not be able to provide translations into B/C/S of all of the documents by that date. Therefore, could I respectfully suggest that we work to that timetable, and if by Tuesday, say, midday, it transpires that not all of the documents have been translated, the relevant parts of the documents, have been translated into B/C/S, then I communicate that to my learned colleague and to Chambers when, at that stage, we expect that we can provide the relevant portions in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, you have to bear in mind that the accused have the right to a fair and expeditious trial, and he has the right to read all those supporting materials in a language that he could understand. We appreciate the effort you made to furnish all those supporting materials as early as possible, and I understand there's no problem for you to provide those materials in the original language by Tuesday afternoon. And as much as the materials which has been already translated into the B/C/S. So I hope that you could file us a report to see how much work you need for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, Your Honour, I should also indicate that I don't expect that CLSS will be able to assist us at all, because of their considerable backlog. So we will be utilising resources within the Office of the Prosecutor to provide a translation where we don't yet have one, and of course the redactions will be made on the documents by Tuesday. When would you require that report by? Would that be Tuesday lunchtime or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Tuesday lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And it is our intention to make a ruling on those issues; I mean, the motion for the joinder of the two cases, by summer recess. So if you do not fulfil the target date for the disclosure, there will be 14 days for the Defence to respond to that motion. So there's very limited time at our disposal to make any decisions concerning with that motion before the summer recess. I just hope you could bear that in mind. As to the detention issues, these are the presentations of both parties. The Trial Chamber ordered the accused to be detained during the pre-trial proceedings before this Tribunal. We accept the request made by the accused to be detained on remand in the Republic of Croatia on the Tribunal's authority. We also request the Government of the Netherlands to transport the accused to the Schiphol airport as soon as possible and hand him over to the authorities of the Government of the Republic of Croatia. At the same time, we request the Government of the Republic of Croatia to take the accused into custody in the Schiphol airport in the Netherlands and to detain him in Croatia on behalf of the Tribunal, under the following conditions: First, that the rights of the accused under the Statute, the Rules, and the Rules governing the detention of persons awaiting trial on appeal before the Tribunal or otherwise detained under authority of the Tribunal are fully respected. 2: That the accused does not leave the prison in which he's detained without express consent of the Chamber. 3: The accused is being offered adequate medical services according to his health-related needs. Fourth: All communication between the accused and any other person except his Defence counsel and his co-counsel be monitored by the Croatian authorities and that every attempt by the accused to influence or pose a danger to any victim or witness in this case be effectively interrupted and reported immediately to the Registrar of the Tribunal, and that regular reports are submitted to the Registrar by the Croatian authorities on all communications between the accused and the persons outside that prison other than his counsels. The accused is brought back to the seat of the Tribunal at Chamber's order at any time. A written order will be issued shortly by the Chamber to that effect. Mr. Norac, do you have anything to say at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How about your health?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... and you may sit down, please. At this stage, are there any other matters that the parties would like to raise? From the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. From the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, this concludes the Initial Appearance. The case is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Initial Appearance adjourned at
